world.setting: New York City suburb, Beecher Prep middle school and the Pullman family home

auggie.name: August Pullman
auggie.role: protagonist — 10-year-old boy with a craniofacial condition, starting fifth grade at Beecher Prep for the first time
auggie.look: small, ten-year-old boy with a distinctive craniofacial difference — misaligned jaw and brow, warm brown eyes, unruly dark brown hair, jeans and a hoodie, carries himself with quiet confidence once he finds his footing

via.name: Via Pullman
via.role: Auggie's older sister — a high-school freshman who has spent years being invisible in her brother's shadow
via.look: fifteen-year-old girl, slender, long dark brown hair pulled back, expressive dark eyes, oversized plaid shirt and dark jeans, quietly serious

jack.name: Jack Will
jack.role: Auggie's first real friend — initially recruited by Tushman, he genuinely chooses Auggie's side after the Halloween betrayal
jack.look: ten-year-old boy, average build, sandy blond hair, open freckled face, blue striped t-shirt and jeans, fidgets with his hands when uncertain

summer.name: Summer Dawson
summer.role: girl who sits with Auggie on the first day out of genuine kindness — not pity, not a dare
summer.look: ten-year-old girl, medium build, warm brown skin, tight curly hair in two puffs, bright yellow t-shirt and purple jeans, laughs easily

julian.name: Julian Albans
julian.role: the bully — popular, handsome, runs a whisper campaign against Auggie that stays just under adult radar
julian.look: ten-year-old boy, well-built, neatly combed dark hair, preppy polo shirt, expensive sneakers, a smile that does not reach his eyes

charlotte.name: Charlotte
charlotte.role: the neutral — knows what is wrong but protects her own social standing instead of acting
charlotte.look: ten-year-old girl, slight, straight blonde hair in a neat ponytail, pink cardigan over white top, always holding a notebook, guarded expression

tushman.name: Mr. Tushman
tushman.role: middle school principal — well-meaning architect of Auggie's welcome, installs 'moral training wheels' by choosing Auggie's first friends
tushman.look: fifties, trim build, salt-and-pepper hair, reading glasses on a lanyard, navy blazer and khakis, gentle eyes behind an official smile

isabel.name: Isabel Pullman
isabel.role: Auggie's mother — former children's book illustrator, devoted but also complicit in her son's over-protection
isabel.look: early forties, warm brown hair in a loose bun, paint-stained fingers she never quite cleans, floral blouse and cardigan, always looks like she is about to say something and decides not to

signatureObjects.name: The Astronaut Helmet
signatureObjects.why: Auggie wore a full astronaut helmet as a child so strangers would stop staring; it is the book's central image of invisibility-as-protection and the moment he removes it permanently is his threshold crossing. No shared icon depicts this.

signatureObjects.name: Charlotte's Looseleaf Paper
signatureObjects.why: The three-column list — Jack's side, Julian's side, 'the right?' — that visualises the book's central moral question as a social ledger. Unique to this story.

signatureObjects.name: Choose Kind Sign
signatureObjects.why: Mr. Browne's precept 'Choose Kind' is the book's recurring moral phrase; it needs to appear as legible text on a poster or blackboard, not reducible to any existing icon.

beecher_hallway.look: bright middle-school corridor — rows of grey lockers, linoleum floor, fluorescent overhead light, busy with fifth-graders

classroom.look: Beecher Prep fifth-grade classroom — wooden desks in rows, chalkboard with precepts, maps on the walls

pullman_home.look: warm Brooklyn brownstone interior — mismatched furniture, children's drawings on the fridge, family photos crowding every surface

forest_camp.look: Broarwood Nature Camp at night — tall dark pines, a clearing lit by a projector screen for the outdoor movie, sleeping bags, flashlights

via_bedroom.look: Via's small bedroom — theatre posters taped to the wall, script pages on the desk, a single lamp, muffled voices through the wall

cafeteria.look: Beecher Prep cafeteria — long tables, plastic trays, loud and crowded, one round table near the windows where Auggie eats alone until Summer arrives

spine.claim: August Pullman is the fixed moral test — every other character is a variable bouncing off his face.
The school's arranged kindness unravels: Jack's overheard betrayal and Julian's invisible campaign reveal the gap between performed and real decency.
Via's invisible cost and Charlotte's calculated neutrality prove that the test touches the whole family, not just the classroom.
The nature retreat is the book's moral crucible — older kids choosing to defend Auggie shows that real kindness is a decision, not an instinct.
The graduation reframe: the award is not for Auggie, it is for everyone in the room — and for the reader who just took the same test.
